lead: A distributed system is a set of computers that work together and appear as one service. A distributed database stores data across those computers. A distributed ledger is a replicated, append-only database whose updates are validated by shared rules, not only by one administrator. Banks, UPI switches and supply-chain platforms use these ideas. This chapter separates three terms students often merge: distributed system, distributed database and distributed ledger.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.1 for Bitcoin as an example of a distributed ledger.

blocks.text: A distributed system has multiple nodes, each a computer or process, connected by a network. The nodes share work so the system can scale, survive a node failure and serve users in different places. A distributed database is a database whose data is stored on more than one node, but managed as one database.

Four ideas appear in every distributed database. Replication keeps copies of the same data on several nodes. Fragmentation splits tables or rows across nodes. Transparency hides that split from the user, who writes ordinary queries. Concurrency control orders simultaneous transactions so they do not corrupt shared data.

The CAP trade-off says a distributed data store cannot always give all three of consistency (every read sees the latest write), availability (every request gets a response) and partition tolerance (the system works when the network splits). During a partition, a system usually chooses consistency or availability. A bank balance system often chooses consistency; a social feed often chooses availability.

items: Administrator trust: a database administrator can change rules, balances or logs.
Conflict resolution: two sites may accept contradictory updates during a partition.
Reconciliation: after the partition, the system must decide which update wins.
Query needs: joins, indexes and SQL are strengths, but they assume a trusted coordinator.

blocks.text: A ledger is an ordered record of transactions. In double-entry bookkeeping, every transaction has a debit entry and a credit entry, and total debits must equal total credits. That equality catches many errors. A bank's core ledger is a database plus business rules: a withdrawal must not make a balance negative.

A distributed ledger is a replicated, append-only record. Append-only means old entries are not silently edited; a correction is a new entry. Replicated means many participants hold a copy. Shared validation means participants apply the same rules before accepting an entry. Cryptographic linking means changing an old entry changes later links; Unit 2 covers the hash functions that make this work.

blocks.text: Distributed ledger technology (DLT) is the broader family. A blockchain is one DLT design that groups entries into blocks and links each block to the previous one. Not every DLT uses blocks. Replication alone does not make a distributed database a blockchain; shared validation and append-only hash-linked blocks are extra.

The Two Generals problem models agreement over an unreliable link. Two armies must attack at the same time, but messengers may be captured. A general sends a time; the other agrees; the acknowledgment may be lost. No finite exchange of messages makes both generals certain that both will attack. The lesson is that acknowledgment does not create common knowledge.

The Byzantine Generals problem models agreement when some participants may send conflicting messages. Some generals may be traitors who tell one group attack and another retreat. The loyal generals need one plan despite faulty or malicious nodes. A crash fault is a node that stops silently. A Byzantine fault is a node that behaves arbitrarily: it may lie, delay or send different answers to different peers.

Ordinary distributed databases are built mainly for crash faults: replicate data, detect a dead node and recover. A distributed ledger that faces untrusted participants must also handle Byzantine faults. It needs enough independent validators and shared rules so a bad node cannot rewrite history alone. Consensus algorithms for this belong to Unit 3.

spec.title: Replication vs shared validation
spec.aria: Two paths from four sites holding ₹10,000: local withdrawals of ₹8,000 reconcile to −₹6,000, while shared validation rejects the second withdrawal and leaves ₹2,000.

examples.question: A bank runs a distributed database with 4 sites. A customer's balance of ₹10,000 is replicated at all 4 sites. Two withdrawals of ₹8,000 each are accepted locally at site 1 and site 2 at the same time, to be reconciled later. Explain why an overdraft can appear, and how a distributed ledger with shared validation avoids it.
steps: Initial balance B = ₹10,000 at each of the 4 sites.
Site 1 accepts withdrawal W1 = ₹8,000 because its local copy shows ₹10,000 ≥ ₹8,000. Local balance becomes ₹2,000.
Site 2 accepts withdrawal W2 = ₹8,000 because its local copy also shows ₹10,000 ≥ ₹8,000. Local balance becomes ₹2,000.
After reconciliation, apply both withdrawals to the replicated balance: ₹10,000 − ₹8,000 − ₹8,000 = −₹6,000. The account is overdrawn by ₹6,000.
With a distributed ledger, shared validation orders the two withdrawals. First W1 is checked against ₹10,000 and accepted; new balance is ₹2,000.
Next W2 is checked against ₹2,000. Since ₹2,000 < ₹8,000, W2 is rejected. Final balance is ₹2,000.
examples.answer: The naive replicated database ends at −₹6,000, an overdraft of ₹6,000; shared validation accepts only one withdrawal and leaves ₹2,000.

traps: Do not say a distributed database is automatically a blockchain. Replication copies data; shared validation and append-only hash-linked blocks are additional design choices.
Do not use DLT and blockchain as synonyms. DLT is the broader family; a blockchain is one DLT design that uses blocks.
In CAP, partition tolerance is not optional in a real network. The real choice during a partition is usually consistency versus availability.
Crash fault and Byzantine fault are different. A crashed node stops; a Byzantine node may keep running and lie.
Double-entry bookkeeping is not the same as two copies of a database. It is a rule that every transaction has matching debit and credit entries.

quiz.q: Define a distributed database in one sentence.
quiz.a: A distributed database stores its data on multiple nodes but is managed as one database.

quiz.q: Why does replication alone not make a system a blockchain?
quiz.a: Replication only copies data. A blockchain also needs shared validation of updates and an append-only history linked by cryptographic hashes.

quiz.q: A balance of ₹12,000 is replicated at two sites. Site A accepts a ₹7,000 withdrawal and site B accepts a ₹7,000 withdrawal before reconciliation. What is the naive final balance, and what does shared validation do if it orders site A first?
quiz.a: Naive final balance = ₹12,000 − ₹7,000 − ₹7,000 = −₹2,000, an overdraft of ₹2,000. Shared validation accepts A first, leaving ₹5,000; B is rejected because ₹7,000 > ₹5,000, so final balance is ₹5,000.

quiz.q: Why is an administrator a trust point in an ordinary distributed database?
quiz.a: The administrator can change rules, balances or logs. Conflict resolution and reconciliation depend on that trusted coordinator, so participants must trust the operator.

quiz.q: State the difference between a crash fault and a Byzantine fault.
quiz.a: A crash fault is a node that stops silently. A Byzantine fault is a node that behaves arbitrarily, including sending false or conflicting messages.

quiz.q: What does the Two Generals problem show about acknowledgment messages?
quiz.a: It shows that no finite exchange of acknowledgments makes both sides certain that both will act, because the last acknowledgment may be lost.

quiz.q: A ledger network has some nodes that may lie. Why is handling crash faults not enough?
quiz.a: Crash-fault handling assumes faulty nodes stop. Lying nodes keep participating and may send different answers to different peers, so the system needs shared validation that tolerates Byzantine behaviour.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry uses permissioned distributed ledgers where several firms need one shared record but do not want one firm to control it. Research explores weaker consistency models and better reconciliation for wide-area databases.
